name: The Great Camphor of Kamo (Higashimiyoshi)

location.address: 1482 Kamo, Higashimiyoshi, Miyoshi District, Tokushima 779-4701, Japan

access: Free, public park (the surrounding farmland was bought by the town from 1970 and converted into a park around the tree, with a public toilet and a rest house, Ookusu House); no permission or ticket needed.
transport: About 10-15 minutes walk (roughly 500m) northeast from JR Awa-Kamo Station on the JR Tokushima Line.
verify_notes: NOT the same tree as kag_010 (Kagoshima's Kamo no Okusu at Kamo Hachiman Shrine, Aira, 31.766,130.570). This one stands roughly 380km away in Tokushima prefecture, Higashimiyoshi town (formerly Mikamo town), on the former site of Wakamiya Shrine, north bank of the Yoshino River. Designated a national Tennen Kinenbutsu (Natural Monument) in 1926 (Taisho 15, Home Ministry Notice No. 58) and upgraded to national TOKUBETSU tennen kinenbutsu (Special Natural Monument) on 1956-07-19 under the Law for Protection of Cultural Properties, the rarer, higher tier of Japanese natural-monument designation held by only a small number of trees nationwide, and a real marker of fame (also listed in New Japan's 100 Famous Trees and one of Shikoku's 88 Views). Its own town literature says in terms of grandeur and beauty it is said to be the best in Japan, because although its trunk is not the thickest in Japan (waisted/narrowed, so 20th or lower by simple girth), its crown spreads almost perfectly symmetrically 52m east-west and 42m north-south, springing dramatically out of flat riverine farmland with nothing else around it. Strong single-tree-destination candidate under the 2026-08-31 exception; flagging only for an editorial fame judgement call, not for any evidence gap. TRUNK MEASUREMENT IS UNUSUAL: three figures given by the Ministry of Environment survey (2007-11-01, cited identically by both sources): root-spread circumference (nemawari) 23.35m; trunk girth by the Ministry of Environment giant-tree method (measured along the irregular trunk surface at 1.3m, excluding small hollows) 16.72m; and a stricter trunk girth excluding surface undulations 14.10m. girth_cm above uses the Ministry-method 16.72m figure; treat it as measured over a fused, buttressed, irregular trunk rather than a clean round trunk. A 1988 survey recorded 13.0-13.8m at the same point, i.e. roughly 3m of measured growth in the 19 years to 2007, which both sources note as remarkable for a tree already put at about 1000 years old. Vitality: town's own account says the tree declined mid-20th-century from surrounding land development and storm/lightning damage (crown spread once reached 70m before losses), prompting protection efforts from 1970 (buying and re-soiling surrounding farmland), after which vigour recovered; no hollows of note as of the 2007 survey. No dated recent (post-2020) photo confirming current health located this pass, only historical designation and 2007 survey data plus undated recent-looking photos on tourism sites (awanavi.jp, wood.jp); writer should treat this as a long-established, actively protected national monument rather than a freshly re-confirmed sighting.

name: The Sacred Nagi of Kumano Hayatama Taisha

location.address: 1 Shingu, Shingu, Wakayama 647-0081, Japan (within the grounds of Kumano Hayatama Taisha, on the approach path to the shrine gate, opposite the Kumano Shinpokan treasure hall)
location.neighbourhood: Shingu, within Kumano Hayatama Taisha shrine grounds

access: Free. Stands on the public sando (approach path) inside the grounds of Kumano Hayatama Taisha, a working Shinto shrine open to visitors during normal daylight hours; no ticket needed to see the tree itself (a separate treasure hall/museum on site, Kumano Shinpokan, charges its own admission but that is unrelated to viewing the tree).
transport: About 15 minutes on foot, or about 5 minutes by car/taxi, from JR Shingu Station (JR West/JR Central Kisei Main Line).
verify_notes: below floor, needs the single-tree-destination judgement call, though the case for it is strong: designated a national Tennen Kinenbutsu (Natural Monument) on 1940-02-10, one of only 4 nationwide Nagi (Nageia nagi) sites/trees ever given that designation and one of only 2 designated as an individual tree rather than a stand/grove (the other being the Kusu of Dazaifu Tenmangu). It stands inside Kumano Hayatama Taisha, one of the three grand shrines of Kumano Sanzan and a core constituent property of the UNESCO World Heritage Site 'Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range' (Kumano Kodo). Selected for 'New Japan's 100 Famous Trees' (1990, timed to the Expo commemorating the same). Reliably described (shrine's own site and Japanese Wikipedia both) as the largest Nagi tree in Japan. Carries a specific historical legend: the Heike Monogatari-derived tradition that the Taira samurai Taira no Shigemori personally planted it in 1159 (Heiji 1) after praying for victory at Kumano on the way to suppress the Heiji Rebellion, using nagi leaves from this same holy site as a battle charm; a sapling from this tree was also planted in Okinawa in 1972 to mark the prefecture's reversion to Japan, which is a live, ongoing cultural connection rather than only ancient history. SPECIES NOTE: this is Nageia nagi (a broadleaf conifer, Podocarpaceae), not to be confused with any other tree also called nagi; it is a MALE (dioecious) individual. GIRTH/SIZE: sources disagree slightly by measurement method. Japanese Wikipedia (citing the Agency for Cultural Affairs designation record): root-spread circumference (nemawari) approx 5.45m, breast-height girth (medori, ~1.2m) approx 4.45m, height approx 17.6m. The shrine's own site gives a vaguer 'height in the low tens of meters' and repeats the ~1000-year age and 'Japan's largest' claim without its own numeric girth. girth_cm above uses the more precise Wikipedia/Bunkacho breast-height figure (445cm); note the larger 545cm root-spread figure in case the writer prefers that instead, and say clearly which measurement point is meant. STRUCTURE: botanically interesting rather than a simple single trunk: Wikipedia's account (citing the botanist Suganuma Takayuki) describes the trunk surface as showing multiple longitudinal grooves with no single clear main stem, viewed from most angles it appears to be roughly 5 fused/grown-together stems, all confirmed to be the same (male) sex, which is treated as remarkable rather than as several separate trees; treat as one collectible point, one shrine tree with one obvious place to stand, not an ensemble. AGE: 'estimated close to 1000 years' per Wikipedia; a search-engine AI summary separately surfaced a conflicting '850 years' figure not found on either fetched source page, so per the search-summary-is-a-lead-not-a-source rule that figure is not used, but age_min is widened to 850 to cover it rather than silently discarding it. No blocking evidence gaps; only outstanding question is the destination-worthiness call, and the UNESCO World Heritage setting plus the four-only national-monument tier make a strong case that it clears it.
